title: How headlights got brighter, whiter, and more blinding after dark
gist: Ars Technica traces automotive glare to a structural shift, not driver behavior: the industry's move from warm halogen reflectors to compact, cool-white LED and HID projectors concentrates light in smaller packages, while the SUV/pickup mix raises mounting height, so even correctly aimed low beams hit smaller-car eyelines. Skoda engineers concede several of their projects run close to regulatory intensity limits (in compliance), and that today's residual glare comes largely from matrix systems whose cameras misrecognize objects and whose computing chain has latency.

themes.theme: LED physics, not driver misuse, drives the glare

insights.claim: The perceived surge in headlight glare is driven by the industry's substitution of halogen reflectors with LEDs, HID projectors and adaptive systems over the past two decades, not by drivers leaving high beams on more often.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Frames glare as a durable product-design externality of the LED transition rather than a behavioral fad, so regulatory and litigation pressure lands on OEMs and lighting-module suppliers, not drivers.
insights.quote: The obvious assumption is that drivers are simply leaving their high beams on more often, but the reality is more complicated.
insights.locator: Anyone who has driven at night in the last

insights.claim: LED compactness is a double-edged design property: it lets stylists build thinner housings and more aggressive front-end designs, but it also concentrates the emitting source intensely, which is the physical root of the dazzle problem.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Styling demand and glare are coupled — any fix that spreads the source area fights the front-end design language OEMs are currently selling, so expect software/optics fixes rather than a retreat to larger emitters.
insights.quote: Their compactness allows designers to create thinner headlights and more aggressive front-end styling, but it also means the light source itself becomes intensely concentrated.
insights.locator: Modern systems have an entirely different engineering goal

insights.claim: Automakers deliberately shifted headlights to cooler, daylight-white color temperatures because humans perceive those wavelengths as sharper and more detailed at night, accepting more glare and discomfort in rain or on poorly marked roads as the trade-off.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The glare is a chosen spec, not a defect — meaning it is reversible by regulation on correlated color temperature, a lever no US rule currently pulls.
insights.quote: The downside is that blue-white light also produces more glare and discomfort, especially in rain or on poorly marked roads.
insights.locator: Automakers have additionally shifted toward cooler color temperatures

insights.claim: Old halogen reflector housings from the 1980s through early 2000s were inefficient and scattered light indiscriminately but 'failed gracefully' — poor visibility without the risk of assaulting an oncoming driver's eyes — a robustness property the LED transition traded away.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Graceful-degradation framing is the argument plaintiffs and regulators will use against LED modules; it also explains why aftermarket halogen-to-LED retrofits are the most dangerous segment.
insights.quote: But they tended to fail gracefully. Visibility wasn’t exceptional, but neither was the likelihood of accidentally assaulting an oncoming driver’s eyes.
insights.locator: Older halogen setups, particularly the reflector housings

insights.claim: The SUV and pickup truck boom mounts headlights higher off the ground than on older sedans, so even correctly aimed low beams shine directly into the eyeline of drivers in smaller vehicles.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Glare exposure scales with the light-truck share of the fleet, so the problem compounds mechanically as long as the US mix keeps shifting toward trucks — a headwind for any purely optical fix.
insights.quote: even correctly aimed low beams can shine directly into the eyeline of drivers in smaller vehicles
insights.locator: Add in the current SUV and pickup truck boom

insights.claim: An escalation effect is at work in automotive lighting: heavier, faster, quieter cars with driver-assistance systems encourage confident nighttime highway driving, which pushes manufacturers to continuously increase forward illumination distance and beam intensity.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A ratchet, not an equilibrium — brightness competition will not self-correct without a binding cap, so watch for photometric rulemaking as the only circuit-breaker.

themes.theme: Skoda: OEMs run near the regulatory ceiling

insights.claim: Skoda, a VW brand, acknowledged that several of its projects operate close to the regulatory limits for low-beam intensity while remaining in full compliance.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: If mainstream OEMs are already at the ceiling, any tightening of intensity limits forces a hardware redesign cycle across model lines rather than a software recalibration.
insights.locator: Regarding whether there are incentives that push companies

insights.claim: Skoda says the primary engineering constraint has inverted with the LED transition: where halogen and HID design centered on protecting surrounding plastic parts from heat, LED design is about protecting the LED from itself and cooling it across driving scenarios, with the trade-off set between performance and cost.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Thermal management, not optics, is where headlight BOM cost and supplier differentiation now sit — a read-through for LED thermal-substrate and driver-IC suppliers.
insights.quote: Now, with LED, the main task is to protect the LED from itself and cool them right in all driving scenarios, with the optimal trade-off being the performance and cost.
insights.locator: “With halogen and HID, the main goal was to protect the plastic parts”

insights.claim: Skoda identifies light intensity — the relationship between light output and beam pattern — as the main cause of glare at greater distances, rather than mounting height or aim alone.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Points the fix at photometric caps on intensity rather than at aim inspections, which is the cheaper but less effective enforcement path regulators usually take.
insights.locator: Skoda says the main cause of glare at greater distances

insights.claim: Skoda claims taller vehicles carry no higher glare risk at distance and that its engineers do not design differently for higher-mounted headlights, adjusting only the initial inclination — 1.1 or 1.2 percent versus the 1 percent standard for low-mounted units.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The OEM position directly contradicts the article's own eyeline argument — a live disagreement over whether ride height should trigger different photometric requirements, and the fault line any future rulemaking will run along.
insights.quote: The only thing we can play with is initial inclination
insights.locator: So what about taller vehicles like semi-trucks, SUVs, and vans?

insights.claim: LED headlight units must be replaced whole when a cluster malfunctions because of much tighter tolerances than halogen sources, and their higher intensities and contrasts make them far more sensitive to misalignment than halogen lights.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Turns a consumable bulb into a module-level replacement — inflating collision-repair severity and insurance loss costs, and creating recurring high-margin parts revenue for OEMs and lighting suppliers.
insights.locator: Now, if an LED cluster malfunctions

themes.theme: The FARS numbers cut against the glare panic

insights.claim: US Fatality Analysis Reporting System data for 2019 to 2023 attributes 46,154 road fatalities to crashes at night in non-lit areas, of which only 446 were due to glare impeding the driver's vision.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Glare is under 1 percent of dark-road fatalities — a hard ceiling on how much a glare-focused rule can move the safety needle, and a reason regulators may prioritize illumination over glare suppression.
insights.quote: 46,154 fatalities on US roads were due to crashes at night and in non-lit areas. 446 were due to glare impeding the driver’s vision.
insights.locator: According to 2019 to 2023 Fatality Analysis Reporting System

insights.claim: 108 of the recorded fatalities occurred among drivers aged 65 and older, which the author uses to explain Florida's fifth-place ranking as an elderly-driver multiplier effect rather than pure traffic volume.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Age-related glare recovery is a demand driver for adaptive and lower-intensity beam options in aging markets, and a demographic tailwind for the glare-complaint political constituency.
insights.locator: A significant share of recorded fatalities, 108 in total

themes.theme: Ratings pressure worked where federal standards froze

insights.claim: An IIHS study found vehicles with 'good'-rated headlights were involved in 19 percent fewer nighttime crashes and 23 percent fewer pedestrian crashes than vehicles with lower-rated systems.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Quantifies the safety payoff of premium lighting, giving OEMs a marketing-defensible reason to keep pushing output — and insurers a rating variable tied to headlight grade.
insights.quote: vehicles with “good”-rated headlights were involved in 19 percent fewer nighttime crashes and 23 percent fewer pedestrian crashes than those with lower-rated systems
insights.locator: An IIHS study found that vehicles

insights.claim: Headlight rating quality improved dramatically once rated: only one of more than 80 systems tested in 2016 earned a 'good' rating, versus roughly 51 percent by model year 2025, while 'marginal' or 'poor' systems fell from 82 percent to about 16 percent.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A clean natural experiment showing third-party ratings, not federal rulemaking, reset OEM incentives — the template for how any future glare metric would actually get adopted.
insights.quote: Only one of more than 80 headlight systems tested in 2016 earned a “good” rating, but by model year 2025, that figure had risen to roughly 51 percent
insights.locator: The 1997 system effectively reset industry incentives

insights.claim: US federal headlight brightness standards have gone largely unchanged since 1997, and adaptive driving beam headlights were only permitted in the US in 2022, decades after the underlying technology existed.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A ~25-year regulatory freeze means the US fleet is only now beginning an ADB retrofit cycle Europe started far earlier — a multi-year content-per-vehicle uplift for lighting suppliers.
insights.quote: US federal headlight brightness standards have remained largely unchanged since 1997. In 2022, however, the US finally allowed adaptive driving beam headlights.

themes.theme: Adaptive matrix beams: the fix that isn't yet

insights.claim: Adaptive matrix headlights that selectively dim portions of the beam are theoretically the solution to glare, but adoption remains inconsistent, regulations vary by country, and many vehicles still rely on brute-force brightness instead of precision.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The technology exists but the market has not converged — regulatory fragmentation, not engineering, is what gates the addressable market for matrix lighting modules.
insights.quote: The result is that nighttime driving increasingly feels less like navigating through darkness and more like surviving a rolling photonics demonstration from the consumer electronics industry.
insights.locator: Adaptive matrix headlights, which can selectively dim portions

insights.claim: Skoda attributes residual blinding by technologically advanced cars mostly to adaptive and especially matrix systems whose camera fails to recognize objects correctly, compounded by latency in the computing chain — a perception-stack failure, not an optics failure.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Puts headlight glare in the same failure class as ADAS perception errors, meaning improvement depends on sensor and inference-stack quality — the same suppliers and the same bottlenecks.
insights.locator: Despite featuring fancier technology, some modern cars still blind drivers
